$comment: Text rules shared by the TypeScript and C# engines. Patterns are compiled case-insensitive with Unicode support. Word boundaries and \d are ASCII-only in both engines.

rules.title: Artificial deadline
rules.explanation: Scammers set short deadlines so you act before you have time to check. Real organisations rarely demand action within hours.

rules.title: Threat of consequences
rules.explanation: Messages that threaten suspension, fines or legal action are designed to trigger fear. Contact the organisation through its official app or number instead.

rules.title: Request for secrecy
rules.explanation: Being told to keep something secret isolates you from people who could warn you. Legitimate employers and banks do not ask for this.

rules.title: Asks you to sign in or verify your account
rules.explanation: A message that asks you to "verify" or "confirm" an account through a link is the classic phishing pattern. Open the official app or type the address yourself.

rules.title: Pushes you to click a link
rules.explanation: "Click here" on its own is common in newsletters, so this is a weak signal. It matters when combined with urgency or account requests.

rules.title: Generic greeting
rules.explanation: Companies you have an account with usually address you by name. A generic greeting suggests a message sent to thousands of people.

rules.title: Asks for a one-time code
rules.explanation: One-time codes prove that you are approving something. Anyone who asks you to share one is trying to log in or pay as you. No real company asks for these.

rules.title: Asks for sensitive personal data
rules.explanation: Card numbers, CVV codes, ID scans and bank logins let criminals steal money or your identity. Never share them in reply to a message.
patterns: \b(social security( number)?|ssn|national (id|insurance)( number)?|passport (number|copy|scan|photo)|(copy|scan|photo) of your (id|passport|driver'?s licen[cs]e)|mother'?s maiden name|date of birth)\b

rules.title: Asks you to pay a fee first
rules.explanation: Requests to pay a small fee, deposit or charge before you receive a parcel, job, prize or refund are the core of advance-fee fraud.

rules.title: Untraceable payment method
rules.explanation: Gift cards, crypto and wire services are requested because payments cannot be reversed or traced. Legitimate businesses do not demand them.
patterns: \b(gift ?cards?|itunes cards?|google play cards?|steam cards?|western union|moneygram|wire transfer)\b

rules.title: Job that sounds too easy
rules.explanation: Offers that need no experience, no interview and pay for trivial tasks like liking videos are common in task and recruitment scams.

rules.title: Moves you to a private chat
rules.explanation: Fake recruiters push conversations to Telegram, WhatsApp or Signal, where there is no company record and accounts disappear easily.

rules.title: Equipment or check payment scheme
rules.explanation: A new "employer" who sends you a check to buy equipment from their vendor is running a fake-check scam: the check bounces after you have paid.

rules.title: Unrealistic earnings promise
rules.explanation: Guaranteed profits or high pay for little effort do not exist. These promises are the hook for investment, task and job scams.

rules.title: Prize or reward you did not enter for
rules.explanation: You cannot win a lottery or giveaway you never entered. "Claim your prize" messages usually lead to a fee request or a phishing page.

rules.title: Crypto investment pitch
rules.explanation: Unsolicited crypto "opportunities", trading platforms and mentors are the leading form of investment fraud. Deposits are rarely recoverable.

rules.title: Parcel delivery problem
rules.explanation: Fake "failed delivery" messages are among the most common SMS scams. Check the tracking number on the carrier's official website instead.
patterns: \b(package|parcel|shipment|delivery|order)\b.{0,60}\b(failed|on hold|held|pending|could not be delivered|unable to deliver|undeliverable|returned|awaiting payment|incomplete address)\b
